summary.text: Prime-adic valuation estimates first establish the needed factorial divisibility; if composite \(n\) has an odd prime divisor \(p\), counting multiples of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) among the factors \(2^k-1\) supplies an extra factor of \(p\), while if \(n=2^r\), Legendre’s digit-sum formula gives \(v_2(a(n-1))=r-1\); in either case the assumed divisibility forces an impossible additional divisibility of a power of \(2\). If \(n\) is prime but \(2\) is not primitive, then \(d=\operatorname{ord}_n(2)<n-1\), so the factor \(2^d-1\), together with coprimality of \((n-1)!\) and \(n\), implies \(n\mid a(n-1)\), and the hypothesis would force the odd prime \(n\) to divide a power of \(2\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(j)=\frac{2^{j-1}}{j!}\prod_{k=1}^{j-1}(2^k-1)\qquad(j\ge 1).
\]
We prove that for every integer \(n>2\),
\[
n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}
\]
implies that \(n\) is prime and that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\).

Throughout, for a prime \(p\) and a positive integer \(x\), write \(v_p(x)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in \(x\). We will repeatedly use the following standard facts.

1. For nonzero integers \(x,y\),
\[
v_p(xy)=v_p(x)+v_p(y).
\]

2. Legendre's formula gives
\[
v_p(t!)=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{t}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Equivalently, if \(s_p(t)\) is the sum of the base-\(p\) digits of \(t\), then
\[
(p-1)v_p(t!)=t-s_p(t).
\]
In particular, when \(t>0\),
\[
(p-1)v_p(t!)<t. \tag{1}
\]
For \(p=2\), this says \(v_2(t!)=t-s_2(t)\).

3. If \(p\) is odd and
\[
d=\operatorname{ord}_p(2)
\]
is the multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(p\), then \(d\mid p-1\), so \(1\le d\le p-1\). In fact \(d\ge2\), since order \(1\) would give \(2\equiv1\pmod p\), impossible for \(p\ge3\). Moreover,
\[
d\mid k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p\mid 2^k-1. \tag{2}
\]

We first record a valuation estimate for the product of the numbers \(2^k-1\).

### Lemma 1: the order-counting estimate

Let \(p\ge3\) be prime and let \(d=\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\). For every integer \(L\ge1\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{L}{d}\right\rfloor
\le
\sum_{k=1}^{L}v_p(2^k-1). \tag{3}
\]

Indeed, among \(1,2,\ldots,L\) are precisely
\[
d,2d,\ldots,\left\lfloor\frac Ld\right\rfloor d.
\]
For each of these indices, (2) shows that the corresponding term \(2^k-1\) is divisible by \(p\), and hence has \(p\)-adic valuation at least \(1\). Every other summand has nonnegative valuation. Summing proves (3).

### Lemma 2: integrality of the displayed formula

For \(n>2\), put
\[
N_n=2^{n-2}\prod_{k=1}^{n-2}(2^k-1),
\qquad F_n=(n-1)!.
\]
Then
\[
F_n\mid N_n. \tag{4}
\]
Consequently,
\[
a(n-1)=\frac{N_n}{F_n},
\qquad
N_n=a(n-1)F_n. \tag{5}
\]

To prove (4), it suffices to compare the valuation at every prime.

First take \(p=2\). Every factor \(2^k-1\) is odd, while
\[
v_2(2^{n-2})=n-2.
\]
Thus
\[
v_2(N_n)\ge n-2.
\]
On the other hand, applying (1) with \(t=n-1>0\) and \(p=2\) gives
\[
v_2((n-1)!)<n-1,
\]
and therefore, since valuations are integers,
\[
v_2(F_n)\le n-2\le v_2(N_n). \tag{6}
\]

Now let \(p\ge3\) be prime and set \(d=\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\). Since \(p\nmid 2\), the factor \(2^{n-2}\) contributes no \(p\)-adic valuation. By Lemma 1, with \(L=n-2\),
\[
v_p(N_n)
=
\sum_{k=1}^{n-2}v_p(2^k-1)
\ge
\left\lfloor\frac{n-2}{d}\right\rfloor. \tag{7}
\]
Since \(d\le p-1\), inequality (1) gives
\[
d\,v_p((n-1)!)
\le
(p-1)v_p((n-1)!)
<n-1.
\]
The left side is an integer, so
\[
d\,v_p((n-1)!)\le n-2.
\]
Because \(d>0\), this is equivalent to
\[
v_p(F_n)\le \left\lfloor\frac{n-2}{d}\right\rfloor. \tag{8}
\]
Combining (7) and (8) yields \(v_p(F_n)\le v_p(N_n)\). Together with (6), this holds for every prime \(p\), proving \(F_n\mid N_n\).

This also establishes directly that the rational-looking defining expression for \(a(n-1)\) is an integer and gives identity (5).

We now assume
\[
n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}. \tag{9}
\]
We first rule out composite \(n\), and then handle the primitive-root assertion once primality is known.

## Excluding composite numbers with an odd prime divisor

Suppose \(n\) is composite and has an odd prime divisor \(p\). Write
\[
n=mp.
\]
Because \(n\) is not itself the prime \(p\), we have \(m\ge2\). Let
\[
d=\operatorname{ord}_p(2).
\]
We will prove
\[
v_p(N_n)\ge v_p((n-1)!)+1. \tag{10}
\]
By (5) and additivity of valuations, (10) will imply \(p\mid a(n-1)\).

We first establish the factorial identity
\[
v_p((mp-1)!)=v_p((m-1)!)+(m-1). \tag{11}
\]
This follows immediately from Legendre's formula. Indeed,
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p((mp-1)!)
&=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{mp-1}{p^i}\right\rfloor\\
&=(m-1)+\sum_{i\ge2}\left\lfloor\frac{mp-1}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(i\ge2\), division by \(p^i\) gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{mp-1}{p^i}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{p^{i-1}}\right\rfloor.
\]
Summing these terms gives (11).

Apply (1) to \((m-1)!\). Since \(m-1>0\) and \(d\le p-1\),
\[
d\,v_p((m-1)!)
\le (p-1)v_p((m-1)!)
<m-1.
\]
Hence
\[
d\,v_p((m-1)!)\le m-2. \tag{12}
\]
Also \(d\le p-1\), so
\[
dm\le (p-1)m. \tag{13}
\]
Using (11), (12), and (13), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
d\bigl(v_p((mp-1)!)+1\bigr)
&=d\bigl(v_p((m-1)!)+(m-1)+1\bigr)\\
&=d\,v_p((m-1)!)+dm\\
&\le (m-2)+(p-1)m\\
&=mp-2.
\end{aligned} \tag{14}
\]
Since \(d>0\), (14) implies
\[
v_p((mp-1)!)+1
\le
\left\lfloor\frac{mp-2}{d}\right\rfloor. \tag{15}
\]

On the other hand, Lemma 1 with \(L=mp-2=n-2\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(N_n)
&=v_p\left(2^{mp-2}\prod_{k=1}^{mp-2}(2^k-1)\right)\\
&=\sum_{k=1}^{mp-2}v_p(2^k-1)\\
&\ge \left\lfloor\frac{mp-2}{d}\right\rfloor,
\end{aligned} \tag{16}
\]
because the odd prime \(p\) does not divide the power of \(2\). Combining (15) and (16) proves (10).

Identity (5) says
\[
N_n=a(n-1)(n-1)!.
\]
Both factors are positive, so additivity of valuations and (10) give
\[
v_p(a(n-1))
=v_p(N_n)-v_p((n-1)!)\ge1.
\]
Thus
\[
p\mid a(n-1). \tag{17}
\]
Since \(p\mid n\), hypothesis (9) also implies
\[
p\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}.
\]
Subtracting (17), we find
\[
p\mid 2^{n-2}.
\]
As \(p\) is prime, this forces \(p\mid2\), contradicting \(p\ge3\). Therefore a composite \(n\) satisfying (9) cannot have an odd prime divisor.

## Excluding powers of two

Every positive integer with no odd prime divisor is a power of \(2\). Thus the only remaining composite possibility is
\[
n=2^r
\]
for some \(r\ge2\) (the inequality follows from \(n>2\)). We compute the exact \(2\)-adic valuation of \(a(2^r-1)\).

Each number \(2^k-1\) is odd, so
\[
v_2(N_{2^r})=v_2\left(2^{2^r-2}\prod_{k=1}^{2^r-2}(2^k-1)\right)=2^r-2. \tag{18}
\]
Next, by the base-two form of Legendre's formula,
\[
v_2((2^r-1)!)=(2^r-1)-s_2(2^r-1).
\]
The binary expansion of \(2^r-1\) consists of exactly \(r\) ones, so \(s_2(2^r-1)=r\). Hence
\[
v_2((2^r-1)!)=2^r-1-r. \tag{19}
\]
Using (5), (18), and (19),
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_2(a(2^r-1))
&=v_2(N_{2^r})-v_2((2^r-1)!)\\
&=(2^r-2)-(2^r-1-r)\\
&=r-1. 
\end{aligned} \tag{20}
\]
Therefore there is an odd integer \(u\) such that
\[
a(2^r-1)=2^{r-1}u. \tag{21}
\]
(The quotient \(u\) is odd precisely because (20) is the exact valuation.)

For \(r\ge2\), one has
\[
2^r\ge r+2. \tag{22}
\]
This is immediate at \(r=2\), and induction proves it thereafter: if \(2^r\ge r+2\), then \(2^{r+1}=2\cdot2^r\ge2r+4\ge r+3\). In particular,
\[
2^r-r-1\ge1.
\]
We may therefore factor
\[
2^{2^r-2}=2^{r-1}\,2^{2^r-r-1}, \tag{23}
\]
and the second factor on the right is even.

Hypothesis (9), for \(n=2^r\), together with (21) and (23), says
\[
2^r\mid 2^{r-1}\left(u+2^{2^r-r-1}\right).
\]
Cancelling the positive factor \(2^{r-1}\), we obtain
\[
2\mid u+2^{2^r-r-1}. \tag{24}
\]
But \(u\) is odd, whereas \(2^{2^r-r-1}\) is even, so their sum is odd. This contradicts (24). Thus no composite power of two satisfies (9).

Every composite integer either has an odd prime divisor or is a power of two. The two preceding arguments therefore show that \(n\) must be prime.

## Proving that \(2\) is a primitive root

It remains to prove that the now-prime \(n\) has primitive root \(2\). Since \(n>2\), it is an odd prime. Its totient is
\[
\varphi(n)=n-1.
\]
Let
\[
d=\operatorname{ord}_n(2).
\]
The order \(d\) divides \(n-1\). Suppose, for contradiction, that \(2\) is not a primitive root modulo \(n\). Then its order is not \(n-1\), and hence
\[
1\le d<n-1. \tag{25}
\]
By the definition of the order,
\[
2^d\equiv1\pmod n,
\]
so
\[
n\mid 2^d-1. \tag{26}
\]
Because of (25), the factor \(2^d-1\) occurs in
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{n-2}(2^k-1).
\]
Thus (26) implies
\[
n\mid N_n=2^{n-2}\prod_{k=1}^{n-2}(2^k-1). \tag{27}
\]
Using (5), (27) becomes
\[
n\mid a(n-1)(n-1)!. \tag{28}
\]
No integer among \(1,2,\ldots,n-1\) is divisible by the prime \(n\), so
\[
\gcd\bigl(n,(n-1)!\bigr)=1.
\]
Euclid's lemma applied to (28) therefore gives
\[
n\mid a(n-1). \tag{29}
\]
Combining (29) with the original hypothesis (9) yields
\[
n\mid2^{n-2}.
\]
Since \(n\) is prime, this forces \(n\mid2\), hence \(n\le2\), contradicting \(n>2\).

The supposition that \(2\) was not primitive is therefore impossible. Consequently
\[
\operatorname{ord}_n(2)=n-1=\varphi(n),
\]
which says exactly that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\).

We have proved that every \(n>2\) satisfying
\[
n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}
\]
is prime and has \(2\) as a primitive root modulo \(n\), as required.
